intro: Hethersett, a village just south-west of Norwich, has Kett's Oak on the verge of the old road to Wymondham. By tradition the brothers Robert and William Kett addressed their followers under it in 1549, at the start of Kett's Rebellion. It is one of the Tree Council's 50 Great British Trees, held together by iron bands and a timber prop, and free to see from the verge.
meta_description: Kett's Oak, Hethersett: where Robert Kett is said to have rallied the rebels of 1549, one of the 50 Great British Trees.

trees.name: Kett's Oak

location.address: Verge of the B1172 between Hethersett and Wymondham, Norfolk

trees.story:
In 1549, by tradition under this oak, the brothers Robert and William Kett spoke to the men who would follow them into Kett's Rebellion, a rising against the enclosure of common land and the cost of living. The rebels went on to take Norwich. The rebellion failed, and both brothers were hanged.

The reader who sent it to us put it in their own words. This is where the Ketts "addressed their followers in 1549 ahead of what became Kett's Rebellion". The Norfolk Heritage Explorer records it as a veteran oak reputed locally to be that tree, and in 2002 the Tree Council chose it as one of the 50 Great British Trees for the Queen's Golden Jubilee. Whether this trunk is the very one the Ketts stood under, nobody can prove, and nobody has published its age.

It has had help staying up. A split in the trunk was filled with cement, iron bands hold it together, a timber prop takes the weight of a long limb, and in 2020 Norfolk County Council treated its roots with biochar. It stands behind railings on the grass verge of the old road, easy to see as you pass, with fields beyond.
trees.how_to_recognise: A broad, leaning oak behind black railings on the verge of the B1172, one long limb held up by a timber A-frame prop, with an information board at its foot.

question_meta: Kett's Oak near Hethersett, Norfolk: the 1549 rebellion story, its condition, and where to see it.
question_answer: Kett's Oak is a veteran English oak on the B1172 verge between Hethersett and Wymondham in Norfolk. By tradition Robert and William Kett addressed their followers there in 1549, beginning Kett's Rebellion. It is free to see from the roadside.
question_context: Kett's Rebellion of 1549 was a rising in Norfolk against the enclosure of common land and the rising cost of living. Local tradition holds that the brothers Robert and William Kett addressed the men who joined them under this oak on the road between Wymondham and Hethersett, before the rebels marched on Norwich. The rebellion was crushed and both brothers were hanged. The Norfolk Heritage Explorer records the tree as a veteran oak reputed locally to be the one, and in 2002 the Tree Council named it among the 50 Great British Trees for the Queen's Golden Jubilee. No age has been published, and there is no proof this is the original tree. It is in poor condition: a split in the trunk has been filled with cement, iron bands bind it, a timber prop supports a long limb, and Norfolk County Council treated its roots with biochar in 2020. It stands behind railings on the grass verge, beside a busy road.
